1.textbook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy / Guyton & Hall Medical Physiology 14th ed., Ch. 2
1.diagram: FLUID MOSAIC MODEL OF CELL MEMBRANE
1.answer:
1. Fluid Mosaic Model (Singer & Nicolson, 1972):

The cell membrane is a quasifluid dynamic phospholipid bilayer measuring 7.5–10 nm thick, described as "protein icebergs floating in a lipid sea."

  • Phospholipids (~40%): Amphipathic with polar hydrophilic heads (facing ECF and ICF) and non-polar hydrophobic fatty acid tails (facing inward).
  • Cholesterol: Intercalated between phospholipids; stabilizes membrane fluidity.
  • Carbohydrates (~5%): Form the Glycocalyx on outer surface for cell-to-cell recognition and immune protection.
2. Classification & Functions of Membrane Proteins (~55%):
  1. Integral (Transmembrane) Proteins:
    • Channels & Pores: Selective transport (e.g., Aquaporins, Voltage-gated Na⁺/K⁺ channels).
    • Transporters/Carriers: GLUT transporters, Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump.
    • Receptors: Signal transduction (G-protein coupled receptors, Tyrosine kinase).
  2. Peripheral Proteins:
    • Enzymes: Adenylyl cyclase, Alkaline phosphatase.
    • Cytoskeletal Anchors: Spectrin and Ankyrin in RBCs for cell shape.
    • Cell Adhesion Molecules (CAMs): Cadherins and Integrins for tight junctions.

2.textbook: BD Chaurasia General Anatomy / Langman's Medical Embryology 14th ed., Ch. 2
2.diagram:
MITOSIS VS MEIOSIS COMPARISON
Mitosis
1 Division ➔ 2 Identical Diploid (2n) Cells
Meiosis
2 Divisions ➔ 4 Genetically Diverse Haploid (n) Gametes
2.answer:
1. Stages of Mitosis:

Occurs in somatic cells: Prophase (chromatin condenses into chromosomes, nuclear envelope breaks down), Metaphase (chromosomes align at equatorial plate, mitotic spindle attaches to kinetochores), Anaphase (sister chromatids separate to opposite poles), Telophase (nuclear envelopes reform, chromosomes decondense) followed by Cytokinesis.

2. Differences Between Mitosis and Meiosis:
FeatureMitosisMeiosis
LocationSomatic cellsGerm cells (gonads)
DivisionsOne divisionTwo divisions (Meiosis I & II)
Daughter Cells2 genetically identical diploid (2n) cells4 genetically distinct haploid (n) gametes
Crossing OverAbsentPresent in Pachytene of Prophase I
FunctionGrowth, tissue repair, regenerationGamete formation, genetic diversity
3. Clinical Importance of Non-Disjunction:

Failure of homologous chromosomes (Meiosis I) or sister chromatids (Meiosis II/Mitosis) to separate properly leads to Aneuploidy:

  • Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome): 47, XX/XY, +21 (associated with advanced maternal age).
  • Trisomy 18 (Edwards Syndrome) & Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome).
  • Klinefelter Syndrome (47, XXY) & Turner Syndrome (45, X0).

3.textbook: BD Chaurasia General Anatomy / Guyton 14th ed. Ch. 2
3.diagram: Outer Membrane ➔ Intermembrane Space ➔ Inner Folded Cristae ➔ Matrix (ATP Synthase, mtDNA)
3.answer:
Structure and Functions of Mitochondria:
  • Double Membrane: Smooth permeable outer membrane (porins) and selectively permeable inner membrane folded into Cristae containing Electron Transport Chain (ETC) complexes and ATP synthase particles (F0-F1 complexes).
  • Mitochondrial Matrix: Contains enzymes for Krebs (TCA) cycle, beta-oxidation of fatty acids, circular maternal mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), and 70S ribosomes.
  • Functions: Cellular respiration and ATP generation ("Powerhouse of the cell"), intrinsic apoptosis pathway (via Cytochrome c release), urea synthesis (early steps), and thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue.
  • Clinical Relevance: Maternally inherited Mitochondrial Myopathies (MELAS syndrome, Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy - LHON).
3.bangla: 💡 বাংলা হেল্প নোট: মাইটোকন্ড্রিয়া কেবল মায়ের দিক থেকে সন্তানের কাছে যায় (Maternal inheritance)। এর ভেতরে ক্রেবস চক্র এবং ক্রিস্টির গায়ে এটিপি তৈরি হয়। সাইটোক্রোম সি রিলিজ করে অ্যাপোপটোসিস নিয়ন্ত্রণ করে।

4.textbook: Robbins Basic Pathology 10th ed. / BD Chaurasia General Anatomy
4.diagram: Acid Hydrolases (pH ~4.5–5.0) ➔ Primary Lysosome ➔ Secondary Phagolysosome ➔ Residual Body
4.answer:
Lysosomes & Storage Disorders:
  • Structure: Membrane-bound cytoplasmic organelles originating from Golgi complex; contain > 50 acid hydrolases (optimal pH 4.5–5.0 maintained by $H^+$ ATPase proton pump).
  • Functions: Heterophagy (phagocytosis of bacteria), Autophagy (recycling of worn-out organelles), Autolysis (cellular self-destruction).
  • Lysosomal Storage Diseases (LSDs): Autosomal recessive inherited deficiency of specific lysosomal enzymes causing insoluble substrate accumulation:
    • Tay-Sachs Disease: Hexosaminidase A deficiency ➔ GM2 ganglioside accumulation (cherry-red spot in macula, neurodegeneration).
    • Gaucher Disease: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency ➔ Glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages ("crumpled tissue paper" cytoplasm, splenomegaly, bone crises).
    • Niemann-Pick Disease: Sphingomyelinase deficiency ➔ Sphingomyelin accumulation (foamy histiocytes, hepatosplenomegaly).
4.bangla: 💡 বাংলা হেল্প নোট: লাইসোজোম হলো কোষের সুইসাইডাল ব্যাগ ও পরিচ্ছন্নতাকর্মী। নির্দিষ্ট এনজাইম না থাকলে যে উপাদান হজম হওয়ার কথা তা কোষে জমে যায়—একে লাইসোজোমাল স্টোরেজ ডিজিজ (Tay-Sachs, Gaucher, Niemann-Pick) বলে।

5.textbook: BD Chaurasia General Anatomy / Langman's Embryology Ch. 2
5.diagram: Formula: Number of Barr Bodies = (Total Number of X Chromosomes) - 1
5.answer:
Barr Body & Lyon's Hypothesis:
  • Definition: Inactive, condensed, heterochromatic sex chromatin mass seen at the periphery of the nucleus in female somatic cells (or as a "drumstick" appendage in neutrophil nuclei).
  • Lyon Hypothesis (Mary Lyon, 1961): In somatic cells of female mammals, one of the two X chromosomes is randomly inactivated around the 16th day of embryonic development, achieving dosage compensation between males (XY) and females (XX).
  • Formula: Number of Barr bodies = Total X chromosomes − 1.
    • Normal female (46, XX): 1 Barr body.
    • Normal male (46, XY): 0 Barr body.
    • Turner Syndrome (45, X0): 0 Barr body.
    • Klinefelter Syndrome (47, XXY): 1 Barr body.
    • Triple X Syndrome (47, XXX): 2 Barr bodies.
5.bangla: 💡 বাংলা হেল্প নোট: মেয়েদের দুইটা X ক্রোমোজোমের একটা নিষ্ক্রিয় হয়ে গুটিয়ে নিউক্লিয়াসের দেয়ালে সেক্স ক্রোমাটিন বা বার বডি তৈরি করে। বার বডির সংখ্যা = (X ক্রোমোজোমের মোট সংখ্যা − ১)। পুরুষদের বার বডি থাকে না (০)।

6.textbook: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 21st ed. / BD Chaurasia Genetics
6.diagram: Trisomy 21 (95% Maternal Meiotic Non-disjunction) ➔ 47, XX/XY, +21
6.answer:
Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21):
  • Karyotypes: 95% Pure Trisomy 21 (47, XX/XY, +21 due to maternal meiotic non-disjunction); 4% Robertsonian Translocation (e.g., t(14;21)); 1% Mosaicism.
  • Craniofacial Features: Flat facial profile, brachycephaly, upward slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, Brushfield spots on iris, low-set ears, macroglossia with protruding tongue.
  • Musculoskeletal & Dermatoglyphics: Generalized hypotonia, hyperflexible joints, single transverse palmar crease (Simian crease), wide sandal gap between 1st and 2nd toes.
  • Internal Systemic Malformations:
    • Congenital Heart Defects (50%): Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD / Endocardial cushion defect), VSD.
    • GIT: Duodenal atresia ("double-bubble" sign), Hirschsprung disease.
    • Other: Intellectual disability, early-onset Alzheimer's disease (due to amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21), 10–20x increased risk of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL).
6.bangla: 💡 বাংলা হেল্প নোট: ২১ নম্বর ক্রোমোজোমে ৩টি কপি থাকে। মায়ের বয়স ৩৫-এর বেশি হলে ঝুঁকি দ্রুত বাড়ে। প্রধান লক্ষণ: চ্যাপ্টা মুখ, সিমিয়ান ক্রিজ (হাতের তালুতে সোজা একটি রেখা), জিভ বের হয়ে থাকা, এবং হার্টে AVSD ডিফেক্ট।

8.diagram:
AXILLARY ARTERY BRANCHES (PECTORALIS MINOR AS LANDMARK)

Superior Thoracic Artery

8.answer:
1. Boundaries and Contents of the Axilla:
  • Apex (Cervicoaxillary canal): Bounded anteriorly by clavicle, posteriorly by superior border of scapula, medially by outer border of 1st rib.
  • Base: Formed by skin, superficial fascia, and thick axillary fascia.
  • Anterior Wall: Pectoralis major, Pectoralis minor, Subclavius muscle, and clavipectoral fascia.
  • Posterior Wall: Subscapularis, Teres major, and Latissimus dorsi.
  • Medial Wall: Upper 4–5 ribs with intercostal muscles and Serratus anterior muscle.
  • Lateral Wall: Intertubercular sulcus of humerus, Coracobrachialis, and Biceps brachii.
  • Contents: Axillary artery and its branches, Axillary vein and tributaries, Cords and terminal branches of Brachial Plexus, 5 groups of Axillary lymph nodes (Anterior, Posterior, Lateral, Central, Apical), and Axillary fat.
2. Course and Branches of the Axillary Artery:

Continuation of the Subclavian artery at the outer border of the 1st rib; terminates at the lower border of Teres major muscle to become the Brachial artery. Divided into 3 parts by the Pectoralis minor muscle:

  • 1st Part (Above Pectoralis minor - 1 Branch): Superior Thoracic Artery.
  • 2nd Part (Behind Pectoralis minor - 2 Branches):
    • Thoracoacromial Artery: Pierces clavipectoral fascia and gives 4 branches (Pectoral, Acromial, Clavicular, Deltoid - Mnemonic: PAC-D).
    • Lateral Thoracic Artery: Accompanies long thoracic nerve, supplies lateral breast.
  • 3rd Part (Below Pectoralis minor - 3 Branches):
    • Subscapular Artery: Largest branch, gives circumflex scapular branch.
    • Anterior Circumflex Humeral Artery.
    • Posterior Circumflex Humeral Artery: Traverses quadrangular space with Axillary nerve.

9.textbook: BD Chaurasia Human Anatomy Vol 1 / Snell's Clinical Anatomy
9.diagram: Carpal Tunnel: 9 Tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL) + 1 Median Nerve under Flexor Retinaculum
9.answer:
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome:
  • Anatomy: An osteofibrous canal formed by the concavity of carpal bones (floor/sides) roofed by the thick Flexor Retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament).
  • Contents (10 structures): Median nerve + 9 long flexor tendons (4 Flexor Digitorum Superficialis, 4 Flexor Digitorum Profundus, 1 Flexor Pollicis Longus).
  • Etiology: Compression of the Median nerve due to synovitis, rheumatoid arthritis, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, or repetitive wrist flexion.
  • Clinical Signs:
    • Paresthesia, numbness, and burning pain over lateral 3½ fingers (palmar surface). Note: Palm sensation is spared because palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to flexor retinaculum!
    • Thenar muscle wasting (Ape-thumb deformity).
    • Tinel's Sign: Percussion over flexor retinaculum reproduces tingling.
    • Phalen's Test: Unforced maximum wrist flexion for 60 seconds reproduces symptoms.
  • Treatment: Wrist splints, local steroid injection; surgical release of flexor retinaculum.

13.answer:
📌 1. Anatomical Boundaries, Roof, and Floor of the Femoral Triangle

The Femoral Triangle (Scarpa's Triangle) is a triangular subfascial depression situated in the upper one-third of the front of the thigh immediately below the groin crease.

A. Anatomical Boundaries:

  • Superior Boundary (Base): Formed by the Inguinal Ligament (Poupart's ligament), which extends from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic tubercle.
  • Medial Boundary: Formed by the medial border of the Adductor Longus muscle.
  • Lateral Boundary: Formed by the medial border of the Sartorius muscle.
  • Apex: Directed downwards; formed by the point where the Sartorius muscle crosses the Adductor Longus; it is continuous inferiorly with the Adductor Canal (Hunter's canal).

B. Roof of the Triangle:

Formed from superficial to deep by:

  • Skin.
  • Superficial fascia: Contains superficial inguinal lymph nodes, the terminal segment of the Great Saphenous Vein, and superficial branches of the femoral artery (superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac, superficial external pudendal).
  • Cribriform fascia (pierced by the great saphenous vein) and deep fascia of the thigh (Fascia Lata).

C. Floor of the Triangle (Gutter-shaped from Lateral to Medial):

  • Formed by four muscular bellies sloping down into a central gutter:
    1. Iliopsoas (most lateral).
    2. Pectineus.
    3. Adductor Longus (most medial).
    4. (Adductor brevis may rarely form a small part of the floor between pectineus and adductor longus).

⚡ 2. Contents of the Femoral Triangle (Lateral to Medial: "NAVL")

Arranged from lateral to medial across the base of the triangle:

  • 1. Femoral Nerve (L2, L3, L4):
    • Lies deeply in the groove between the Psoas major and Iliacus muscles.
    • High-Yield Anatomical Rule: The Femoral Nerve lies OUTSIDE (lateral to) the Femoral Sheath! It splits into anterior and posterior terminal branches within the triangle.
  • 2. Femoral Artery and its Branches:
    • Traverses the center of the triangle from midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis (midinguinal point).
    • Gives off the Profunda Femoris Artery (Deep Artery of Thigh), which arises from its lateral aspect ~3.5 cm below the inguinal ligament.
  • 3. Femoral Vein and its Tributaries:
    • Lies medial to the femoral artery at the base of the triangle, but passes posterior to the artery at the apex.
    • Receives the Great Saphenous Vein (passing through the saphenous opening) and the profunda femoris vein.
  • 4. Deep Inguinal Lymph Nodes & Femoral Canal: Embedded within the medial compartment of the femoral sheath.
  • 5. Lateral Cutaneous Nerve of the Thigh (L2, L3): Crosses the lateral angle of the triangle.
  • 6. Femoral Branch of the Genitofemoral Nerve (L1, L2): Pierces the anterior wall of the femoral sheath to supply skin over the triangle.

🔍 3. The Femoral Sheath and Femoral Canal

A. Femoral Sheath Architecture:

  • A downward-projecting, funnel-shaped fascial tube extending 3 to 4 cm into the thigh behind the inguinal ligament.
  • Embryological Origin: Formed anteriorly by the downward prolongation of the Fascia Transversalis (lining abdominal wall) and posteriorly by the Fascia Iliaca (lining posterior pelvic wall).
  • Internal Subdivisions: Subdivided by two anteroposterior vertical fibrous septa into three distinct compartments:
    • Lateral Compartment: Contains the Femoral Artery and femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve.
    • Intermediate Compartment: Contains the Femoral Vein.
    • Medial Compartment: Represents the small, conical Femoral Canal.

B. Anatomy of the Femoral Canal & Femoral Ring:

  • Dimensions: Approximately 1.25 cm (0.5 inch) long and 1.25 cm wide at its base.
  • Contents: Loose areolar and adipose tissue, efferent lymphatic channels, and the Deep Inguinal Lymph Node of Cloquet (Rosenmüller).
  • The Femoral Ring (Upper Abdominal Opening / Base):
    • Anterior: Inguinal ligament.
    • Posterior: Pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament) overlying the pectineal line of the pubic bone.
    • Medial: The sharp, rigid, crescentic free edge of the Lacunar Ligament (Gimbernat's ligament)!
    • Lateral: Thin fibrous septum separating it from the Femoral Vein.

⚠️ 4. Why Femoral Hernia is More Common in Females and Highly Prone to Strangulation

A. Predilection for Females (Female:Male Ratio $\approx 4:1$):

1. Wider Female Bony Pelvis: The gynecoid pelvis has a significantly broader transverse pelvic diameter, which dramatically widens the subinguinal space and increases the cross-sectional area of the femoral ring.
2. Smaller Caliber Femoral Vessels: Females have smaller diameter femoral arteries and veins compared to males, leaving a relatively larger dead space within the medial femoral canal.
3. Multiparity: Repeated pregnancies cause persistent intra-abdominal hypertension, stretching of the abdominal musculature, and structural laxity of pelvic fascial condensations.

B. Extreme Vulnerability to Strangulation (Surgical Emergency!):

Femoral hernia has the highest rate of strangulation (up to 40-50%) among all abdominal wall hernias because of the following rigid anatomical factors:

  • Rigid Unyielding Boundaries: The femoral ring is small (barely 1.25 cm) and completely enclosed by unyielding osteofibrous structures: the rigid inguinal ligament anteriorly, the hard bone and Cooper's ligament posteriorly, and especially the razor-sharp, unyielding crescentic edge of the Lacunar Ligament (Gimbernat's ligament) medially.
  • Narrow Hernial Neck: As hernial contents enter the narrow canal, venous outflow is instantly obstructed. Rapid edema ensues, leading to acute arterial strangulation and gangrene within hours.
  • Richter's Hernia: Frequently only a portion of the antimesenteric circumference of the small intestine is trapped. Intestinal lumen obstruction is absent (patient may still pass flatus/feces), delaying diagnosis until fatal perforation occurs!
13.bangla:
🎓 ফিমোরাল ট্রায়াঙ্গেল (Femoral Triangle): গঠন ও বাউন্ডারি

Femoral Triangle (Scarpa's Triangle) হলো উরুর ওপরের এক-তৃতীয়াংশে অবস্থিত একটি ত্রিকোণাকার অবনমিত এলাকা।

১. এর সীমানা মনে রাখার সহজ কৌশল:

  • ওপরে (Base): Inguinal Ligament (কুঁচকির লিগামেন্ট)।
  • ভেতরের দিকে (Medial): Adductor Longus পেশির ভেতরের সীমানা।
  • বাইরের দিকে (Lateral): Sartorius পেশির ভেতরের সীমানা।
  • মেঝে (Floor): চারটি পেশি দিয়ে তৈরি হয় (বাইরে থেকে ভেতরে: Iliopsoas $\rightarrow$ Pectineus $\rightarrow$ Adductor Longus)।

⚡ ফিমোরাল ট্রায়াঙ্গেলের উপাদান: "NAVL" ফর্মুলা

বাইরে থেকে ভেতরের দিকে (Lateral to Medial) সাজানো থাকে:

  • N - Nerve: Femoral Nerve (সবচেয়ে বাইরে থাকে)।
    ভাইভায় সবচেয়ে বড় ফাঁদ: ফিমোরাল নার্ভ কিন্তু Femoral Sheath এর ভেতরে থাকে না! এটি শিথের বাইরে সোয়াস পেশির খাঁজে থাকে।
  • A - Artery: Femoral Artery (ম্যাসিভ পালস পাওয়া যায়, এখান থেকে বের হয় Profunda Femoris Artery)।
  • V - Vein: Femoral Vein (এখানে Great Saphenous Vein এসে ড্রেন করে)।
  • L - Lymphatics (Femoral Canal): ফিমোরাল ক্যানাল ও লিম্ফ নোড (Node of Cloquet)।

⚠️ ফিমোরাল হার্নিয়া কেন নারীদের বেশি হয় এবং পচে যায় (Strangulation)?

১. নারীদের কেন ৪ গুণ বেশি হয়?

• মেয়েদের পেলভিসের হাড় অনেক বেশি চওড়া (Broad Pelvis) হওয়ায় ফিমোরাল রিংয়ের ফাঁকা জায়গা পুরুষের চেয়ে অনেক বড় থাকে।
• মেয়েদের রক্তনালীগুলো পুরুষের চেয়ে কিছুটা সরু হওয়ায় পাশে ফাঁকা স্পেস বেশি থাকে।
• বারবার সন্তান জন্ম দেওয়ার কারণে তলপেটের পেশি ও লিগামেন্ট ঢিলে হয়ে যায়।

২. কেন ফিমোরাল হার্নিয়া সবচেয়ে বেশি পচে যায় (Strangulation)?

সব ধরণের হার্নিয়ার মধ্যে ফিমোরাল হার্নিয়াতেই গ্যাংগ্রিন হওয়ার ঝুঁকি সবচেয়ে বেশি (প্রায় ৪০-৫০%)। কারণ ফিমোরাল রিংটি মাত্র সোয়া এক সেন্টিমিটার চওড়া এবং এর চারপাশ শক্ত হাড় ও ছুরির মতো ধারালো লিগামেন্ট দিয়ে ঘেরা:
• সামনে শক্ত ইনগুইনাল লিগামেন্ট।
• পেছনে পিউবিক হাড়ের কুপার্স লিগামেন্ট।
• ভেতরের দিকে ক্ষুরধার লাকুনার লিগামেন্ট (Lacunar Ligament)!
অন্ত্রের একটি ছোট অংশ এই ছোট ফাঁদ দিয়ে গলে যাওয়ার সাথে সাথেই ধারালো লাকুনার লিগামেন্টে আটকে গিয়ে রক্ত চলাচল বন্ধ হয়ে যায় এবং কয়েক ঘণ্টার মধ্যে নাড়ি পচে গ্যাংগ্রিন হয়ে ফুটো হয়ে যায়। তাই ফিমোরাল হার্নিয়া পাওয়া মাত্রই কোনো দেরি না করে সাথে সাথে ইমার্জেন্সি অপারেশন করতে হয়!

14.answer:
1. Anatomy of the Inguinal Canal:

An oblique intramuscular passage ~4 cm long in the lower anterior abdominal wall, running downwards and medially just above the medial half of the inguinal ligament. Extends from the Deep Inguinal Ring (oval opening in fascia transversalis 1.25 cm above midinguinal point) to the Superficial Inguinal Ring (triangular gap in external oblique aponeurosis above pubic crest).

  • Anterior Wall: External oblique aponeurosis throughout; reinforced laterally by Internal oblique.
  • Posterior Wall: Fascia transversalis throughout; reinforced medially by Conjoint Tendon (falx inguinalis).
  • Roof: Arched fleshy fibers of Internal oblique and Transversus abdominis.
  • Floor: Grooved upper surface of Inguinal ligament; reinforced medially by Lacunar ligament.
  • Contents: Spermatic Cord in males (or Round Ligament of Uterus in females), Ilioinguinal nerve (traverses canal and exits superficial ring).
2. Direct vs Indirect Inguinal Hernia:
FeatureIndirect Inguinal HerniaDirect Inguinal Hernia
OriginEnters Deep Ring (patent processus vaginalis)Directly pushes through Hesselbach's triangle
Relation to Inf. Epigastric ArteryLateral to Inferior Epigastric ArteryMedial to Inferior Epigastric Artery
Age GroupYounger males / congenitalElderly males (weak abdominal wall)
Deep Ring Occlusion TestHernia is controlled / preventedHernia still protrudes medially

CORONARY CIRCULATION SCHEMATIC
Right Coronary Artery (RCA)

Left Coronary Artery (LCA)

19.answer:
Arterial Blood Supply of the Heart:

Arises from the ascending aorta immediately above the aortic valve cusps (Aortic sinuses of Valsalva):

  • Right Coronary Artery (RCA):
    • Origin: Anterior aortic sinus.
    • Course: Runs down right atrioventricular groove, curves around inferior border to posterior AV groove.
    • Branches: (1) SA nodal artery (supplies SA node in 60%), (2) Right marginal artery (along acute margin), (3) AV nodal artery (in 80–90%), (4) Posterior Interventricular Artery (PIVA / PDA).
    • Territory: Right atrium, most of right ventricle, posterior 1/3 of interventricular septum, inferior wall of LV, SA and AV nodes.
  • Left Coronary Artery (LCA):
    • Origin: Left posterior aortic sinus.
    • Branches: (1) Left Anterior Descending (LAD) / Anterior Interventricular artery ("Widow-maker" artery), (2) Circumflex artery (curves in left AV groove, gives Left marginal branch).
    • Territory: Left atrium, most of left ventricle, anterior 2/3 of interventricular septum, apex of the heart, AV bundle branches.
  • Cardiac Dominance: Determined by which artery gives off the Posterior Interventricular Artery (PIVA). If from RCA = Right Dominant (approx. 85–90% of individuals). If from Circumflex branch of LCA = Left Dominant (approx. 10%). Co-dominant in ~5%.

- উইডো-মেকার (Widow-maker): LAD ব্লকে সবচেয়ে বেশি হঠাৎ মৃত্যু ঘটে কারণ এটি হার্টের সবচেয়ে কাজের অংশ বাম ভেন্ট্রিকল ও সেপ্টামের সামনের দুই-তৃতীয়াংশে রক্ত দেয়।

20.diagram:
BRONCHOPULMONARY SEGMENTS (10 IN RIGHT, 10 IN LEFT)
Right Lung (10 Segments)
Upper (3) + Middle (2) + Lower (5)
Left Lung (10 Segments)
Upper/Lingular (5) + Lower (5)
20.answer:
1. Definition & Anatomical Characteristics:

A Bronchopulmonary Segment is a functionally, anatomically, and surgically independent unit of lung tissue aerated by a tertiary (segmental) bronchus.

  • Each segment is pyramid-shaped with apex pointing toward the hilum and base on the pleural surface.
  • It has its own segmental bronchus, segmental branch of pulmonary artery, and bronchial vessels running centrally together.
  • The pulmonary veins run in the intersegmental planes (drain adjacent segments), serving as surgical guides during segmental resection.
2. Enumeration of Segments:
Right Lung (10 Segments):
- Superior Lobe (3): Apical, Posterior, Anterior.
- Middle Lobe (2): Lateral, Medial.
- Inferior Lobe (5): Superior (apical of lower), Medial basal, Anterior basal, Lateral basal, Posterior basal.
Left Lung (10 Segments):
- Superior Lobe (5): Apical, Posterior, Anterior, Superior lingular, Inferior lingular.
- Inferior Lobe (5): Superior (apical of lower), Medial basal, Anterior basal, Lateral basal, Posterior basal.
3. Surgical & Clinical Importance:

Enables segmentectomy (resection of a diseased segment, e.g., in localized bronchiectasis or early lung cancer) without sacrificing the healthy adjacent lung tissue. Important in postural drainage of lung abscesses.

26.answer:
1. Peritoneal & Visceral Relations of the Stomach:
  • Anterior Relations: Anterior abdominal wall, Left costal margin, Left lobe of liver, Diaphragm.
  • Posterior Relations (Stomach Bed): Separated from posterior surface by lesser sac: (1) Diaphragm (left crus), (2) Left Kidney, (3) Left Suprarenal gland, (4) Body and tail of Pancreas, (5) Tortuous Splenic Artery, (6) Transverse Mesocolon, (7) Spleen (gastrosplenic ligament).
2. Arterial Blood Supply:

Derived entirely from branches of the Celiac Trunk:

  • Lesser Curvature: Left Gastric artery (from celiac trunk) and Right Gastric artery (from hepatic artery proper).
  • Greater Curvature: Right Gastro-omental (Gastroepiploic) artery (from gastroduodenal) and Left Gastro-omental artery (from splenic artery).
  • Fundus: 5–7 Short Gastric arteries (from splenic artery in gastrosplenic ligament).
3. Lymphatic Drainage & Clinical Relevance:
  • Drains into 4 territories corresponding to arteries: Left gastric nodes, Right gastric nodes, Right gastro-omental nodes, and Pancreaticosplenic nodes, all converging into Celiac lymph nodes.
  • Troisier's Sign & Virchow's Node: Enlargement of left supraclavicular lymph node via thoracic duct metastasis from gastric adenocarcinoma.
  • Krukenberg Tumor: Transcoelomic transperitoneal seeding of gastric signet-ring cell carcinoma to both ovaries.

34.diagram: +--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | THE CIRCLE OF WILLIS (CIRCULUS ARTERIOSUS) | +--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ Anterior Communicating Artery (AComA) / \ / \ Left Anterior Cerebral / \ Right Anterior Cerebral (ACA) / \ Left ICA =====+ +===== Right ICA | | Left Middle Cerebral (MCA) <--+ +--> Right Middle Cerebral (MCA) | | Left Posterior \ / Right Posterior Communicating \ / Communicating (PComA) \ / Left Posterior Cerebral\ / Right Posterior Cerebral (PCA) \ / Basilar Artery | Left & Right Vertebral Arteries +--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ COMMON SITES OF BERRY ANEURYSM RUPTURE: 1. AComA junction with ACA: 40% (Most common site!) 2. PComA junction with Internal Carotid: 30% 3. Middle Cerebral Artery bifurcation: 20% +--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
34.answer:
📌 1. Anatomical Formation and Components of the Circle of Willis

The Circle of Willis (Circulus Arteriosus) is a large, polygonal arterial anastomosis situated in the subarachnoid space within the interpeduncular fossa at the base of the brain. It surrounds the optic chiasma, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, and posterior perforated substance.

Constituent Arterial Components (Anterior to Posterior):

  • Anteriorly: Formed by the single midline Anterior Communicating Artery (AComA), which connects the right and left anterior cerebral arteries across the longitudinal cerebral fissure.
  • Anterolaterally: Formed by the right and left Anterior Cerebral Arteries (ACA) (terminal branches of the Internal Carotid Artery).
  • Laterally: Formed on each side by the terminal segment of the Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) just before its division.
  • Posterolaterally: Formed by the right and left Posterior Communicating Arteries (PComA), which run backward from each Internal Carotid Artery to join the corresponding Posterior Cerebral Artery.
  • Posteriorly: Formed by the divergence of the right and left Posterior Cerebral Arteries (PCA), which represent the terminal bifurcation of the midline Basilar Artery (formed by the confluence of the two Vertebral Arteries).

⚡ 2. Communicating Branches & Central Perforating Vessels

A. Communicating Channels:

  • Anterior Communicating Artery: A short vessel (about 4 mm long) forming the vital bridge between the two anterior cerebral circulations.
  • Posterior Communicating Arteries: Vital collateral links connecting the anterior circulation (Internal Carotid system) with the posterior circulation (Vertebrobasilar system).

B. Central (Perforating / Ganglionic) Arterial Groups:

Small, slender nutrient vessels arise from the circle and plunge into the brain substance to supply the basal ganglia, thalamus, and internal capsule:

  • Anteromedial Group: Arise from ACA and AComA; enter the anterior perforated substance to supply the anterior hypothalamus and rostrum of corpus callosum.
  • Anterolateral (Striate) Group: Arise predominantly from the initial segment of the Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA). Includes the Lateral Striate Arteries (Charcot's Artery of Cerebral Hemorrhage), which supply the posterior limb of the internal capsule, caudate nucleus, and putamen. Rupture leads to classical contralateral hemiplegia!
  • Posteromedial Group: Arise from the PCA and PComA; enter the posterior perforated substance to supply the mammillary bodies, thalamus, and subthalamus.
  • Posterolateral Group: Arise from the PCA; supply the posterior thalamus (pulvinar) and geniculate bodies.

🎓 3. Functional Significance of the Circle of Willis

  • Collateral Anastomotic Reservoir: Provides an equalizing hemodynamic manifold. Under normal physiological conditions, little or no blood mixes across the communicating vessels because pressures in the contributing arteries are roughly equal.
  • Protective Bypass against Cerebral Ischemia: If one internal carotid artery or vertebral artery becomes progressively stenosed or acutely occluded (by atherosclerosis or embolus), the communicating channels dilate, allowing blood from the contralateral carotid or vertebrobasilar systems to cross over and nourish the ischemic cerebral hemisphere, thereby preventing massive cerebral infarction.

⚠️ 4. Berry Aneurysms and Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH)

A. Etiology & Common Anatomical Sites:

  • Pathogenesis: Berry (saccular) aneurysms arise from a congenital focal weakness in the tunica media and internal elastic lamina, exacerbated over time by hemodynamic stress and arterial hypertension.
  • Predisposing Conditions: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and Coarctation of the Aorta.
  • Most Frequent Locations:
    1. Anterior Communicating Artery junction with ACA (40% - Most common site).
    2. Posterior Communicating Artery junction with Internal Carotid (30%) (often compresses Cranial Nerve III, producing ipsilateral oculomotor nerve palsy with ptosis and a dilated, fixed pupil!).
    3. Bifurcation of the Middle Cerebral Artery (20%).

B. Clinical Consequences of Aneurysm Rupture:

  • Acute Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH): Arterial blood extravasates under high pressure into the subarachnoid cisterns.
  • Classic Presentation: Sudden onset of excruciating, explosive headache, classically described by the patient as "the worst headache of my life" (Thunderclap Headache), reaching peak intensity within seconds.
  • Associated Clinical Signs: Nausea, projectile vomiting, transient loss of consciousness, neck stiffness (meningism), positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs, photophobia, and subhyaloid retinal hemorrhages on fundoscopy.
  • Delayed Complications:
    • Cerebral Vasospasm (Days 4 to 14): Blood breakdown products trigger arterial vasospasm leading to delayed ischemic neurological deficits. Prevented with oral Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days.
    • Obstructive or Communicating Hydrocephalus: Blood clots block CSF flow through arachnoid granulations.
34.bangla:
🎓 সার্কেল অফ উইলিস: মস্তিষ্কের রক্ত সরবরাহের জাদুকরী রিং

Circle of Willis হলো মস্তিষ্কের নিচে অবস্থিত একটি বহুভুজ বা রিং আকৃতির ধমনীর সংযোগস্থল (Anastomosis)। এটি ইন্টারপেডাঙ্কুলার ফসাতে অপটিক কায়াজমা ও পিটুইটারি গ্ল্যান্ডের ডাঁটার চারপাশে অবস্থিত।

১. এই রিংটি কীভাবে তৈরি হয় (সহজে মনে রাখার ফর্মুলা):

  • সামনে থাকে একটি একক Anterior Communicating Artery, যা দুই পাশের দুটি Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA)-কে যুক্ত করে।
  • দুই পাশে থাকে Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) এবং এর থেকে পেছনের দিকে যাওয়া Posterior Communicating Artery (PComA)।
  • পেছনে থাকে দুটি Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA), যা মূলত হার্ট থেকে আসা দুটি ভার্টিব্রাল আর্টারি মিলে তৈরি হওয়া Basilar Artery এর দুটি শাখা।

⚡ সার্কেল অফ উইলিসের প্রধান কাজ (Functional Significance)

স্বাভাবিক অবস্থায় এই রিংয়ের এক পাশের রক্ত অন্য পাশে খুব একটা যায় না, কারণ সব পাশের প্রেশার সমান থাকে। কিন্তু যদি কোনো কারণে একদিকে রক্তনালী বন্ধ হয়ে যায় (যেমন স্ট্রোক বা এথেরোস্ক্লেরোসিস দিয়ে এক পাশের Internal Carotid Artery ব্লক হয়), তখন সাথে সাথে সার্কেল অফ উইলিসের ফাঁকা নালীগুলো চওড়া হয়ে অপর পাশ ও পেছনের দিক থেকে রক্ত সরবরাহ চালু রাখে। ফলে রোগীর মস্তিষ্কের পুরো একটা গোলার্ধ প্যারালাইসিস হওয়া থেকে রক্ষা পায়।

⚠️ বেরি অ্যানিউরিজম (Berry Aneurysm) ও সাব-অ্যারাকনয়েড হেমোরেজ (SAH)

১. বেরি অ্যানিউরিজম কী এবং সবচেয়ে বেশি কোথায় হয়?

ধমনীর দেয়ালে জন্মগতভাবে মাঝের স্তর (Tunica media) দুর্বল থাকলে রক্তচাপের ধাক্কায় রক্তনালীর সংযোগস্থলে জাম বা বেলের মতো ছোট ছোট ফোসকা তৈরি হয়। একে Berry Aneurysm বলে।

সবচেয়ে কমন সাইট: Anterior Communicating Artery এবং ACA এর সংযোগস্থলে (৪০%)। এর পরেই দ্বিতীয় স্থানে রয়েছে Internal Carotid এবং Posterior Communicating Artery এর সংযোগস্থল (৩০%)।

২. অ্যানিউরিজম ফেটে গেলে রোগীর কী লক্ষণ দেখা দেয়? (Thunderclap Headache):

অ্যানিউরিজম ফেটে সাব-অ্যারাকনয়েড স্পেসে রক্ত ছড়িয়ে পড়াকে Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) বলে। রোগী হঠাৎ প্রচণ্ড মাথা ব্যথায় চিৎকার করে ওঠে, যাকে চিকিৎসা বিজ্ঞানে বলা হয় "The worst headache of my life" বা Thunderclap Headache। এর সাথে ঘাড় শক্ত হয়ে যাওয়া (Neck rigidity), ফটোফোবিয়া এবং বমি হয়।

৩. ভাইভা ও প্রেসক্রিপশন স্পেশাল (Nimodipine কেন দেওয়া হয়?):

অ্যানিউরিজম ফেটে রক্ত জমাট বাঁধলে তার ৩ থেকে ১৪ দিনের মাথায় মস্তিষ্কের রক্তনালীগুলো খিঁচুনি দিয়ে সংকুচিত হয়ে যায় (Cerebral Vasospasm), যার ফলে রোগী সেকেন্ডারি স্ট্রোকে মারা যেতে পারে। এই ভ্যাসোস্পাজম ঠেকাতে রোগীকে সাথে সাথে ক্যালসিয়াম চ্যানেল ব্লকার Nimodipine ৬০ মিগ্রা প্রতি ৪ ঘণ্টা পর পর টানা ২১ দিন খাওয়াতে হয়!

35.answer:
1. Parts, Coverings & Relations of the Thyroid Gland:

Consists of two lateral lobes connected across the midline by an isthmus lying opposite 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings. Covered by: (1) True capsule (fibrous condensation of stroma), (2) False capsule (derived from pretracheal fascia, anchoring it to thyroid and cricoid cartilages via Berry's ligament, which explains why the thyroid moves with swallowing).

2. Arterial Blood Supply & Venous Drainage:
  • Superior Thyroid Artery: First branch of External Carotid Artery; descends to apex of each lobe.
  • Inferior Thyroid Artery: Branch of Thyrocervical Trunk (from 1st part of Subclavian artery); enters base.
  • Thyroidea Ima Artery: Occasional branch (~10%) from brachiocephalic trunk or arch of aorta.
  • Venous Drainage: Superior & Middle thyroid veins (drain into Internal Jugular Vein); Inferior thyroid veins (drain into Left Brachiocephalic vein).
3. Surgical Relationship to Laryngeal Nerves in Thyroidectomy:
  1. Superior Pole: External Laryngeal Nerve runs closely with the Superior Thyroid Artery. Surgical rule: Ligate the artery CLOSE to the superior pole to avoid nerve injury (injury paralyzes cricothyroid muscle ➔ loss of high-pitched voice).
  2. Inferior Pole: Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove intimately related to terminal branches of the Inferior Thyroid Artery. Surgical rule: Ligate the artery AWAY from the gland (trunk ligation) or individually on the capsule to preserve the nerve (injury causes hoarseness; bilateral injury causes acute stridor and airway asphyxia!).
  3. Parathyroid Glands: 4 small glands lying on the posterior border between true and false capsule; must be carefully preserved to prevent life-threatening post-op hypocalcemia and tetany.

📌 1. Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus (Roots, Trunks, Divisions, Cords & Branches)

The Brachial Plexus is a somatic nerve plexus that provides sensory and motor innervation to the entire upper limb and shoulder girdle. It is formed in the posterior triangle of the neck and passes through the cervico-axillary canal into the axilla.

A. Components & Structural Formation:

  • Roots (Ventral Primary Rami): Formed by the anterior primary rami of spinal nerves C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1 (with contributions from C4 in a prefixed plexus, or T2 in a postfixed plexus).
  • Trunks (Pass across posterior triangle):
    • Upper Trunk: Formed by the union of C5 and C6 roots.
    • Middle Trunk: Direct continuation of the C7 root.
    • Lower Trunk: Formed by the union of C8 and T1 roots.
  • Divisions (Lie behind the clavicle):
    Each of the three trunks divides into an Anterior (flexor) and a Posterior (extensor) division (total of 6 divisions).
  • Cords (Named according to their anatomical relationship to the 2nd part of Axillary Artery):
    • Lateral Cord (C5, C6, C7): Formed by the union of the anterior divisions of the Upper and Middle trunks.
    • Medial Cord (C8, T1): Formed by the unjoined anterior division of the Lower trunk.
    • Posterior Cord (C5, C6, C7, C8, T1): Formed by the confluence of the posterior divisions of all three trunks.

B. Branches of the Brachial Plexus:

  • Branches from Roots: Long Thoracic Nerve of Bell (C5, C6, C7 $\rightarrow$ Serratus anterior), Dorsal Scapular Nerve (C5 $\rightarrow$ Rhomboids, Levator scapulae).
  • Branches from Trunks: Suprascapular Nerve (C5, C6 $\rightarrow$ Supraspinatus & Infraspinatus) and Nerve to Subclavius (C5, C6) (both arise from the Upper Trunk).
  • Branches from Lateral Cord: Lateral Pectoral Nerve (C5-C7), Musculocutaneous Nerve (C5-C7), Lateral Root of Median Nerve (C5-C7).
  • Branches from Medial Cord: Medial Pectoral Nerve (C8, T1), Medial Cutaneous Nerve of Arm (T1), Medial Cutaneous Nerve of Forearm (C8, T1), Ulnar Nerve (C8, T1), Medial Root of Median Nerve (C8, T1).
  • Branches from Posterior Cord: Upper Subscapular Nerve (C5, C6), Thoracodorsal Nerve (Nerve to Latissimus Dorsi, C6-C8), Lower Subscapular Nerve (C5, C6), Axillary Nerve (C5, C6), Radial Nerve (C5-T1).

⚡ 2. Erb-Duchenne Palsy (Upper Trunk Injury - C5, C6)

A. Mechanism of Injury:

  • Caused by an excessive increase in the angle between the head and the shoulder, causing severe stretching or tearing of the upper roots/trunk.
  • Common Causes: Difficult childbirth with shoulder dystocia (forceful lateral traction on infant head during vertex delivery), breech delivery with traction on neck, or falling from a motorcycle/horse landing on the shoulder while the head is forced away.
  • Site of Lesion: Erb's Point (the junction where 6 nerves meet: C5 root, C6 root, Upper trunk, suprascapular nerve, nerve to subclavius, and anterior/posterior divisions).

B. Muscles Paralyzed:

Biceps brachii, Brachialis, Brachioradialis, Deltoid, Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, and Supinator.

C. Characteristic Deformity ("Policeman's Tip" / "Porter's Tip" / "Waiter's Tip" Hand):

  • Arm (at shoulder): Hangs by the side, Adducted and Medially Rotated (due to loss of abductors [Deltoid, Supraspinatus] and lateral rotators [Infraspinatus, Teres minor]; unopposed Pectoralis major and Subscapularis draw the arm in).
  • Forearm (at elbow): Extended and Pronated (due to loss of elbow flexors [Biceps, Brachialis] and supinators [Biceps, Supinator]; unopposed Triceps and Pronator teres).
  • Sensory Loss: Cutaneous anesthesia along the outer aspect of the shoulder, lateral arm, and forearm (C5-C6 dermatomes / Axillary and Musculocutaneous sensory distribution).
  • Reflexes Lost: Biceps jerk and Supinator (Brachioradialis) jerk are absent.

⚡ 3. Klumpke's Paralysis (Lower Trunk Injury - C8, T1)

A. Mechanism of Injury:

  • Caused by an excessive upward traction on an abducted arm.
  • Common Causes: Clutching an object (such as a tree branch or windowsill) while falling from a height, or upward pulling on the infant's arm during a difficult breech delivery; also caused by compression by a cervical rib or Pancoast tumor of the lung apex.
  • Site of Lesion: Lower trunk of brachial plexus or anterior primary rami of C8 and T1.

B. Muscles Paralyzed:

  • All intrinsic muscles of the hand (supplied by C8, T1 via ulnar and median nerves): Dorsal and palmar interossei, all 4 lumbricals, thenar muscles, and hypothenar muscles.
  • Flexors of the wrist and fingers (Flexor carpi ulnaris, ulnar half of Flexor digitorum profundus).

C. Characteristic Clinical Presentation:

  • "True Claw Hand" (Main en griffe):
    • Hyperextension at the Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints (due to paralysis of lumbricals and interossei; unopposed Extensor digitorum communis pulls joints back).
    • Flexion at the Proximal and Distal Interphalangeal (PIP and DIP) joints (due to loss of intrinsic extension; unopposed long flexors pull fingers into tight claw).
  • Sensory Loss: Along the medial (ulnar) border of the forearm, wrist, and medial $1\frac{1}{2}$ digits (C8, T1 dermatomes).
  • Associated Horner's Syndrome (Hallmark of T1 root avulsion):
    If the T1 preganglionic sympathetic fibers are torn, the patient develops ipsilateral:
    1. Partial Ptosis (drooping of upper eyelid due to paralysis of superior tarsal muscle).
    2. Miosis (pupillary constriction due to unopposed parasympathetic sphincter pupillae).
    3. Anhidrosis (loss of sweating on ipsilateral face and neck).
    4. Enophthalmos (apparent backward sinking of eyeball into orbit).
